Franklin town clerk resigns after ballot mishap

By Rick Sobey | rick.sobey@bostonherald.com | Boston Herald

PUBLISHED: September 13, 2020 at 5:49 p.m. | UPDATED: September 13, 2020 at 5:50 p.m.

A Massachusetts town clerk has resigned after officials in the 4th Congressional District community lost track of thousands of ballots in the primary earlier this month.

Franklin Town Clerk Teresa Burr on Friday stepped down to “re-establish confidence with the voters of this community in their elections,” she wrote in her resignation letter.

Two days after the Sept. 1 primary, thousands of uncounted ballots surfaced in Franklin as the 4th Congressional District remained too close to call. The newly discovered 3,000 uncounted ballots were mail-in votes that appeared to have never made it to polling locations on Election Day.

Poll workers ended up counting the 3,000 ballots late into the night two days after the primary. Jake Auchincloss eventually won the Democratic primary.

In Burr’s resignation letter, she noted that this election season has been “the most challenging election cycle in my career.”

“I want to assure every resident that my performance over the past few months for this election was not intentional, nor have I ever conspired to deprive any voter of their ability to cast a ballot and have that ballot counted as part of an election,” Burr wrote.

“Any oversights that I made during this election cycle are due to the many challenges this election has brought upon myself,” she added. “I believe it is in the best interest of the community to have a new leadership team in place.”

Officials in three 4th Congressional District communities — Franklin, Newton and Wellesley — two days after the primary restarted counting primary ballots following Secretary of the Commonwealth William Galvin filing a court order to authorize local poll workers to continue counting ballots that were received on time and had not been tallied by the end of primary night.

The chair of the Franklin Town Council thanked Burr for her “many successful years of dedicated service to the town.”

“I want to assure the voters of Franklin that our current Town Clerk office staff, in conjunction with assistance from the Secretary of the Commonwealth’s team, will conduct a flawless election in November and beyond,” Franklin Town Council Chair Thomas Mercer wrote.

All of this creates a strong sense of appoggiatura, or the tendency of chords to "lean" on eachother (or resolve into eachother by halfstepl).

Simple answer to your question. In the key of F, G major is the V of V (five of five). This appears frequently in classical music and jazz.

This is an example of a secondary dominant. G minor is the actual ii chord in F. C is the V of F. The V of C is G. The G major can be borrowed from the key of C and used to resolve back to C which can then obviously be used to resolve back to F.

V of V is the most common secondary dominant, but every chord ii-vi has its own V which can be borrowed and used as a secondary dominant. The F dominant you mentioned would be the V of IV (five of four) because F is the V of Bb.

Look up "secondary chord" on Wikipedia for more detailed info.

Also, here is a quick overview for anyone not familiar with theory or keys. The chords of a key are built from the notes of that key. Typically, three notes, 1-3-5 intervals (or four notes 1-3-5-7 intervals if you want a jazzier sound).

Basically, in the key of F, your notes are F G A Bb C D E F. Starting at each letter, you add more notes by skipping one and adding one, skipping one and adding one. The various major and minor intervals this creates are what makes a chord a specific type of chord.

Example: Start with F note, skip G, add A, skip Bb, add C. Now you have F A C notes which make an F major chord (three note harmony). You can also skip D and add E for F A C E notes which make an F major 7 chord (four note harmony).

Do the same skipping pattern starting with each note of any key to build all the chords of that key. In a major key the chords always come out the same with three note harmony or four note harmony:

I = major or major 7 (in key of F, F major [F A C notes] or F major 7 [F A C E notes])

ii = minor or minor 7 (in key of F, G minor [G Bb D notes] or G minor 7 [G Bb D F notes])

iii = minor or minor 7 (in key of F, A minor [A C E notes] or A minor 7 [A C E G notes])

IV = major or major 7 (in key of F, Bb major [Bb D F notes] or Bb major 7 [Bb D F A notes])

V = major or dominant 7 (in key of F, C major [C E G notes] or C dominant 7 [C E G Bb notes])

vi = minor or minor 7 (in key of F, D minor [D F A notes] or D minor 7 [D F A C notes])

vii = diminished or minor7b5 (in key of F, E diminished [E G Bb notes] or E minor7b5 [E G Bb D notes])

I hope that wasn't too confusing for anyone.

EDIT: I forgot to explain your Bb minor arpeggio. This is another borrowed chord, borrowed from the parallel minor key of F minor. Bb minor is the iv of F minor. This appears frequently in all styles of music.

Google "minor iv chord" for more detailed info.
